lesson.title: Protecting the Ends: Telomeres and the Limits of Replication
lesson.summary: Telomeres are repetitive, protective DNA sequences that cap the ends of linear chromosomes, and they exist because the ordinary mechanism of DNA replication cannot fully copy the very last stretch of a linear DNA molecule.
lesson.body:
Eukaryotic chromosomes, unlike the circular DNA of many bacteria, are linear, which means every chromosome (recall the double helix has two strands running in opposite directions) has two physical ends. That linearity creates a subtle but unavoidable problem for the replication machinery described earlier in this unit, known as the end replication problem.

The issue traces directly back to how the lagging strand is built, as described in the Okazaki Fragments chapter. Each Okazaki fragment begins with an RNA primer that is later removed and replaced with DNA, using the 3' end of the neighboring fragment upstream as a starting point to fill the gap. But at the very end of a linear chromosome, the last fragment's primer sits right at the tip, and once that primer is removed, there is no further fragment upstream of it to extend into the resulting gap. That small stretch simply cannot be filled in. As a result, every time a linear chromosome's lagging strand is replicated, the daughter strand ends up a little shorter than the strand it was copied from.

Telomeres are the cell's solution to this problem, or more precisely, its way of buying time against it. A telomere is a long stretch of a short DNA sequence repeated over and over at each chromosome end. In humans, that repeated sequence is 5'-TTAGGG-3', repeated thousands of times. Because telomeres do not code for any protein, the gradual shortening caused by the end replication problem chips away at expendable repetitive sequence for many rounds of division before it threatens any actual genes.

Some cells also have a way to rebuild lost telomere length using an enzyme called telomerase. Telomerase is unusual because it carries its own internal RNA molecule, which it uses as a template to add additional telomere repeats (more copies of TTAGGG in humans) onto the 3' end of the chromosome, independent of the normal DNA-templated replication process. Telomerase is active in germ cells and certain stem cells, which need to keep dividing over long periods without losing genetic material, and it is often reactivated abnormally in cancer cells, helping explain why those cells can divide indefinitely. In most differentiated adult somatic cells, however, telomerase activity is low or absent, so telomeres shorten a little with each division. This progressive shortening is one of the mechanisms thought to contribute to cellular aging and the limited number of times a normal cell can divide.
